evidence.question_prompt: Is multi-factor authentication required for every employee email account?
evidence.answer_label: Enforced for most users, a few are exempt
evidence.gap_text: A handful of exempt accounts is where attackers go first, and insurers know it. Carriers routinely ask who the exceptions are, and an exempt executive or finance mailbox is the version of this answer most likely to get your quote loaded or declined.
evidence.fix_text: Remove the exemptions. If a specific account genuinely cannot use MFA, document why in writing and restrict what it can reach — carriers accept a documented, contained exception far more readily than an undocumented one.

evidence.question_prompt: Is MFA required for remote access into your network (VPN, remote desktop, or similar)?
evidence.answer_label: Yes — required for all remote access

evidence.question_prompt: Is MFA required for administrator accounts on your core systems?
evidence.answer_label: Yes — all administrator accounts

evidence.question_prompt: What protection is installed on your computers and servers?
evidence.answer_label: EDR software, but nobody is actively watching the alerts
evidence.gap_text: The tool will spot an attack in progress, but only if somebody reads the alert. Ransomware is typically deployed outside business hours precisely because nobody is looking. Insurers ask specifically whether alerts are monitored, and an unmonitored tool earns little credit.
evidence.fix_text: Have your IT provider take on monitoring and response for the alerts, so a detection at 2am produces action rather than an unread notification.

evidence.question_prompt: What percentage of your computers and servers have that protection installed?
evidence.gap_text: The uncovered machines are the ones that will be hit. Underwriters read anything short of near-total coverage as a gap they cannot size, because neither can you.
evidence.fix_text: Reconcile the list of protected machines against your actual asset list and close the difference. The machines missing from an inventory are usually old servers, which are also the most vulnerable ones.

evidence.question_prompt: Is at least one backup copy kept where an attacker on your network cannot reach or delete it?
evidence.answer_label: In a separate cloud service, but reachable with our normal logins
evidence.gap_text: If an attacker takes an administrator login, they can reach the backups with it. Ransomware crews delete backups first and demand payment second — a backup that shares your everyday credentials is one password away from being gone.
evidence.fix_text: Move backups behind credentials that are not used for anything else, and turn on immutability so a copy cannot be deleted or overwritten for a fixed retention window.

evidence.question_prompt: When did you last actually restore data from backup to prove it works?
evidence.answer_label: Never tested / not sure
evidence.gap_text: You do not currently know whether your backups work. Most businesses that discover this discover it during a ransomware attack, when the answer arrives too late to do anything about. An underwriter will read an untested backup as no backup.
evidence.fix_text: Restore a real file and a full system from backup this month and write down what happened, including how long it took. Then repeat quarterly.

evidence.question_prompt: How often is critical business data backed up?
evidence.answer_label: Daily or more often

evidence.question_prompt: Do you use email security filtering beyond what your mail provider includes by default?
evidence.answer_label: Provider built-in protection with the paid security add-on enabled

evidence.question_prompt: Is DMARC configured on your domain to stop others sending email that appears to come from you?
evidence.answer_label: Not configured / not sure
evidence.gap_text: Anyone can send email that appears to come from your business. The common version is a criminal emailing your customers a real-looking invoice with their own bank details — your customers lose money, and they come to you about it. Underwriters check this in seconds because it is public information.
evidence.fix_text: Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for your domain and work up to an enforcing policy. This is a one-off configuration job with no ongoing licence cost.

evidence.question_prompt: How quickly is access removed when someone leaves the business?
evidence.answer_label: When somebody remembers to ask
evidence.gap_text: Former employees may still be able to reach company email and files. Beyond the obvious risk from a disgruntled leaver, these forgotten accounts are unmonitored and unprotected — attackers look for them specifically. It also signals to an underwriter that security depends on memory rather than process.
evidence.fix_text: Create a written leaver checklist, run it the day someone leaves, and audit existing accounts now against your current staff list. That audit usually turns up more than expected.

evidence.question_prompt: Do employees have administrator rights on their own computers?
evidence.answer_label: A small number of documented exceptions
evidence.gap_text: Documented exceptions are acceptable to most carriers, but each one raises the ceiling on how much damage a single mistaken click can do.
evidence.fix_text: Review the exception list periodically and remove rights that are no longer needed. Keep the written justification current — it is what makes this defensible to an underwriter.

evidence.question_prompt: How often do you review who has access to what?
evidence.answer_label: About once a year
evidence.gap_text: An annual review is enough to catch the worst drift but leaves most of the year uncovered. Access accumulates quietly as people change roles.
evidence.fix_text: Move to a quarterly review of who can reach financial systems, customer data and administrative tools, and keep the sign-off.

evidence.question_prompt: How quickly are critical security updates applied after release?
evidence.answer_label: Within 14 days

evidence.question_prompt: Are you still running any software or operating systems that no longer receive security updates?
evidence.answer_label: Yes, but they are isolated from the rest of the network
evidence.gap_text: Isolation is the right interim answer and most carriers will accept it, provided you can describe the isolation. It is still a system that will never be fixed again, so it needs an end date.
evidence.fix_text: Document how the system is isolated and what it can still reach, and set a replacement date. Carriers respond well to a dated plan.

evidence.question_prompt: Do you have a written plan for what to do when a cyber incident happens?
evidence.answer_label: Written down, but never rehearsed
evidence.gap_text: An unrehearsed plan is usually missing the practical details — who has the phone numbers when email is down, who can authorise taking systems offline. Those gaps only show up under pressure, when they cost hours.
evidence.fix_text: Run a one-hour tabletop exercise: talk through a ransomware Monday morning with the people who would actually be involved, and correct the plan where it broke. Keep a dated note that you did it.

evidence.question_prompt: Do you know who to call in the first hour — IT provider, insurer, and legal?
evidence.answer_label: Yes — written down and available offline

evidence.question_prompt: How often do staff receive security awareness training?
evidence.answer_label: Once a year
evidence.gap_text: Annual training is the accepted minimum but decays quickly — recognition of a scam message drops off within a few months of the session.
evidence.fix_text: Move to short quarterly refreshers rather than one long annual session. Retention is markedly better and staff resent it less.

evidence.question_prompt: Do you run simulated phishing tests?
evidence.answer_label: No
evidence.gap_text: Without simulations you have no idea how your staff actually behave when a convincing scam arrives — training completion tells you they sat through it, not that it worked. Carriers increasingly ask for click rates because it is the one measurable human-risk number.
evidence.fix_text: Add phishing simulation, usually bundled with the training platform, and use the results to target follow-up rather than to punish.

evidence.question_prompt: Are laptops and mobile devices encrypted?
evidence.answer_label: Yes — all of them, and we can prove it

evidence.question_prompt: Is sensitive customer or financial data encrypted where it is stored?
evidence.answer_label: Partly / we are not sure where all of it is
evidence.gap_text: Not knowing where sensitive data lives is the more serious half of this answer. After an incident you have to tell people what was exposed, and you cannot do that if you do not know what you held or where.
evidence.fix_text: Map where customer and financial data is stored — including the spreadsheets on individual machines — then apply encryption to those locations.
